For everyday relaxation in people without recent neck surgery or a prescribed rehabilitation plan.

After surgery or with a cervical condition, ask your care team before trying general exercises. Stop if pain increases, or if dizziness, numbness or weakness occurs, and seek medical advice. Stay within a comfortable range; never force or pull your neck.
For everyday screen breaks, not treatment for myopia or an eye condition. Do not press or rub your eyes. Stop if uncomfortable; persistent symptoms need an eye-care assessment.

Comfortable sitting
Find a supported, relaxed position.
Choose a stable seat. Let your feet rest on the floor and support your back.
Let your shoulders settle and keep your head in a comfortable position. Breathe naturally; do not hold a rigid pose.
Change position regularly and take a short screen break. Comfort is more important than holding a perfect pose.
Gentle shoulder circles
Move slowly without forcing.
Sit comfortably and let your arms rest by your sides. Keep breathing naturally.
Gently circle both shoulders in a comfortable range, keeping your neck relaxed.
Pause, then gently reverse direction if comfortable. Stop when you need a rest; do not push through pain.
Comfortable head turns
A slow, small movement within comfort.
Sit upright comfortably, with shoulders relaxed and eyes facing forward.
Slowly turn your head to the left only as far as comfortable, then return to the middle. Do not pull with your hands.
Repeat gently to the right and return to the middle. Stop for pain, dizziness, numbness or weakness.
20-20-20 eye break
Look away from nearby screens.
After about 20 minutes of screen use, pause what you are doing. This guide does not run a timer.
Look at something about 6 metres (20 feet) away for at least 20 seconds. Look at a real distant object, not this screen.
Blink naturally and return when comfortable. Make regular breaks part of your routine.
Natural blinking
Give your eyes a gentle break.
Pause your screen task and relax your face.
Blink naturally and gently. Avoid squeezing, rubbing or pressing your eyes.
If discomfort persists, arrange an eye-care assessment instead of repeating exercises to push through it.
Screen & surroundings
Make text and lighting comfortable.
For a computer monitor, sit about an arm’s length away and place it slightly below eye level.
Enlarge small text and adjust brightness to suit the room. Reduce glare rather than leaning forward.
Relax your shoulders and take regular breaks. These changes support comfort; they do not cure myopia.
Postoperative protection
Prepare questions for your care team.
Read the discharge instructions provided by your surgical team. Keep their contact details accessible.
Ask which activities are restricted, whether a collar is required, and when to contact the team about symptoms. Do not infer these from general exercise cards.
At follow-up, ask when rehabilitation may begin and who will guide it. This preview does not set dates, loads or movement angles.
Return to daily activities
Discuss a personal return-to-activity plan.
Review daily needs such as walking, sitting, sleep and computer use with your care team.
Ask how to pace activity and rest, and when work, driving or lifting may resume. Follow your own instructions.
Request an approved plan before starting neck mobility, strengthening or other rehabilitation. General relaxation cards are not a postoperative prescription.
